# Series 5

The series 4 data appears valid, but suffers from energy growth that was
not previously observed in series 1 though 3. Therefore, the series 4
data will be re-run.

## Velocity Verlet

Added the velocity Verlet update to compensate for the larger time step.
The `revtest()` function shows how effective that is in maintaining
particle positions. Currently running MD2 version 1.5.9. For example:

```{julia}
#| eval: false

julia> MD2.revtest( td, 21, "rf.", 1000, update = "OG", T=Float32, 
                    tau = 0.0177737)
   .
   .
   .
RMS Particle Distance is 0.07083208, 
 3.718950345439551% of lattice spacing of 1.9046256137279147 
 Maximum delta was 0.28849894 on particle 163.
1.2843989f0

julia>  rm.( glob("*.*", td))
7-element Vector{Nothing}:
 nothing
   .
   .
   .
 nothing

julia> MD2.revtest( td, 21, "rfvv.", 1000, update = "VV", T=Float32, 
                    tau = 0.0177737)
   .
   .
   .
RMS Particle Distance is 0.00014607886, 
 0.007669688860197647% of lattice spacing of 1.9046256137279147 
 Maximum delta was 0.0004228177 on particle 30.
5.4627926f-6
```

So the original Verlet algorithm had a mean particle distance of 3.72%
of the lattice spacing, vs. 0.0077% for the velocity Verlet (both run in
`Float32`). Note that the return value is the sum-of-squared distance,
and the velocity Verlet is clearly in the realm of round off error for a
`Float32`. @tbl-revtest shows the results.

| Name     | 64/32 | $\delta t$ | RMS Dist. | \% Lattice | Max Part.  |
|:---------|:-----:|:-----------|:----------|:-----------|:-----------|
| F64      |  64   | 0.01       | 0.0142    | 0.749      | 0.04169    |
| F64013   |  64   | 0.013      | 0.0366448 | 1.92       | 0.176      |
| F640177  |  64   | 0.0177737  | 0.14517   | 7.6218     | 0.37303    |
| F640177b |  64   | 0.0177737  | 0.14485   | 7.605      | 0.43965    |
| F640177c |  64   | 0.0177737  | 0.2774    | 14.5665    | 1.163      |
| F32      |  32   | 0.01       | 0.0170    | 0.89277    | 0.1067     |
| F32013   |  32   | 0.013      | 0.08027   | 4.215      | 0.2677     |
| F320177  |  32   | 0.0177737  | 0.19545   | 10.26      | 0.7719     |
| rf       |  32   | 0.0177737  | 0.0708321 | 3.72       | 0.2885     |
| rfvv     |  32   | 0.0177737  | 0.0001461 | 0.00767    | 0.00042282 |

: `revtest()` results for `Float64` and `Float32` and three different
time steps (runs on 2 October 2025). The last two runs were were
executed on 4 November 2025, the last one with the velocity Verlet
algorithm performing the position and velocity update. Note that
different runs can have different results. All runs had an
initialization temperature of $T=0.03$. {#tbl-revtest}

It is difficult to tell if the momentum is a problem. @fig-MR2 shows it
is not.

```{r}
#| label: fig-MR2

```

We can compare the series 5 max momentum to the previous series
(@fig-MR2b).

```{r}
#| label: fig-MR2b
#| fig-cap: Max momentum of each series.
with( MD2DF.R2, {
   pch = as.factor( series)
   #col = c("blue", "darkred")[pch]
   plot( x = TE.mean.rs, y = M.2.max.raw, pch = as.integer(pch), 
             col = as.integer(pch), panel.first = grid(),
                log = "", ylab = "Max Momentum")
   legend("topright", legend = unique(pch), col = as.integer(unique(pch)), 
          pch=as.integer(unique(pch)))
   })
```

The total energy is also more stable (see @fig-MR2c). As a reminder,
series 2 had a step in the potential energy (the energy at a range of
`rskn = 3.5` was not subtracted from the potential energy equation). The
energy would tend to grow, especially as a ring of particles existed
just outside the `rskn` range when the particles were in their minimum
PE positions. This was fixed before the `S3` runs. Series 4, which
closely duplicated the 1980 work (`Float32` precision and 0.0177737 time
step), suffered from energy growth not seen in 1980. This was due to
longer runs than were possible in 1980 (80k step runs were considered
quite long; series 4 used 4M step runs).

```{r}
#| label: fig-MR2c
#| fig-cap: Total energy range of each series. Series 5 has very little growth.
with( MD2DF.R2, {
   pch = as.factor( series)
   #col = c("blue", "darkred")[pch]
   plot( x = TE.mean.rs, y = TE.max.raw - TE.min.raw, pch = as.integer(pch), 
             col = as.integer(pch), panel.first = grid(),
                log = "", ylab = "TE Range")
   legend("topright", legend = unique(pch), col = as.integer(unique(pch)), 
          pch=as.integer(unique(pch)))
   })
```

@fig-PvTR2 shows the series 5 isochor.

```{r}
#| label: fig-PvTR2
#| fig-cap: Pressure vs. Temperature, with standard deviation and total rnge lines.
plotconfMD2( MD2DF.R2[series == "S5",], x = "ke.mean.rs", y = "Pressure",
             linethresh = 200, main = "Series 5", xlab = "T")
```

On 10 November 2025, I was cleaning up before running a `revtest()` and
I executed the *Julia* command `rm.( glob( "*.*", td))` and,
unfortunately, `td` was defined for data i.e., `.../MD/Data/1980/`), not
testing (`.../MD/dev/MD2J/test/testtemp/`), so all collected raw data
was deleted. A few feeble attempts at restoring the data were made, to
no avail. Only the `S1` and `S2` data were backed up, so `S3`, `S4`, and
`S5` raw data are lost. The collected averages still exist in the MD2
data frames, but there is no ability to back and look at a temperature
or Nelson-Halperin order parameter trajectories.

## Type Error in *Julia* `sqrt()`

Noticed an error in how numbers were typed in *Julia*, whenever the
expression `sqrt(c)` appears where `c` was an integer constant. *Julia*
renders these as `Float64` values, even if the rest of the calculation
is `Float32`, and the `Foat64` would propagate. This was likely not a
major problem, but fixed it in MD2 version 1.6.3.

# Diffusion Runs

The code below will create a list that will be more-or-less easy to
paste into a *Julia* session, along with the run list. The *Julia*
`filerun_thread()` function needs the run-name and the last `*.jld2`
file number.

```{r}
#| label: difflist
#| eval: false
drn <- MD2DF.R4[ series == "S5b", run] # get runs
cat( '["', # create runs string
     paste( drn, collapse = '", "'), '"] \n', sep = "")
# Next line searches td for each run, grabs last, and extracts execution number
lfn <- strsplit( sapply( drn, \(fn) last( list.files( td, 
                                             paste(fn, "*.jld2", sep = ".")))),
                  "[.]")

as.integer(sapply( seq_along( lfn), \(i) lfn[[i]][3]))
```

Following the procedure used in
[FinalDiffusion.pdf](FinalDiffusion.pdf#Diffusion), we need to define
and run some functions.

```{r}
#| label: difffuncs
read_diff <- function( td, runname) { 
   # returns a data.table with diffusion data
   # td is the test data directory
   # runname is a filename ala list.files( td, glob2rx( "*.diff.txt"))
   filename <- list.files( td, runname, full.names = TRUE)
   #print( filename)
   dd <- data.table::fread( filename)
   nrdd <- nrow( dd)
   ddcols <- colnames( dd)
   timecols <- ddcols[ seq.int( from=4, to=length( ddcols), by=3)]
   dscols   <- ddcols[ seq.int( from=5, to=length( ddcols), by=3)]
   dmxcols  <- ddcols[ seq.int( from=6, to=length( ddcols), by=3)]
   dd[, row := 1:nrdd] # adds row number to show time sequence of executions
   dd[, run := rep( runname, nrdd)] # put run name in each row
   reshape( dd, list( timecols, dscols, dmxcols),
            v.names=c("Time", "D2", "Dmax"), timevar="group", idvar="row", 
            drop=c("time","d^2", "max d^2"), direction="long")
} # end read_diff

fitdiff <- function( r, diffdata, plot=FALSE, weights = NULL, verbose = FALSE) { 
   # r is the run id as a string.
   # diffdata is a data.table with fields Time, run, d2mn (mean of the D2 data),
   #     Other fields are ignored.
   dd <- diffdata[ r == run,]
   # print( nrow(dd))
   maxT <- max( dd$Time)
   maxd <- max( dd$d2mn)
   if (!is.null(weights)) weights = 1 / dd$d2sd^2
   
   #lm0 <- lm( d2mn ~ Time - 1, data = dd)
   lm1 <- lm( d2mn ~ Time, data = dd, weights = weights)
   #lm2 <- lm( d2mn ~ poly( Time, 2), data = dd)
 
   if (plot) {
      newT <- data.frame( Time =c( 0, dd$Time)) # Predict value at Time = 0
      pred.w.plim <- predict( lm1, newT, interval = "prediction")
      pred.w.clim <- predict( lm1, newT, interval = "confidence")
      plot( d2mn ~ Time, data = dd, xlim = c( 0, maxT), ylim = c(0, maxd), 
              main = r, xlab = 'Time', ylab = expression( r^2))
      grid()
      if (!is.null( dd$d2sd)) 
         arrows( dd$Time, dd$d2mn - dd$d2sd, dd$Time, dd$d2mn + dd$d2sd,
                 length = 0.05, angle = 90, code = 3)
      matplot(newT, cbind( pred.w.clim, pred.w.plim[, -1]), 
              col = c( 1, 2, 2, 3, 3), lty = c(1,2,2,3,3), type = "l", 
              add = TRUE)
      #abline( lm1)
      abline( h = mean( dd$d2mn), lty = 4, col = 4)
      legend( x = 'bottomright',  pch = c(1, NA, NA, NA, NA), 
              lty = c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4), col = c( 1, 1, 2, 3, 4),
              legend = c("Measurements", 'Regression Line', "Conf. Interval",                            'Pred. Interval', 'Mean'))
   }
   if (verbose) {
      #print( summary( lm0))
      print( summary( lm1))
      #print( summary( lm2))
   }
   nr <- nrow( dd)
   mod <- summary( lm1)
   coeff <- unname( mod$coefficients[ "Time", c( 'Estimate', 'Std. Error')])
   t <- mod$fstatistic
   Fpvalue <-  stats::pf( t['value'], t['numdf'], t['dendf'], lower.tail=FALSE)
   data.table::data.table( run = r, nrd = nr, Estimated = coeff[1], 
      Std.Errord = coeff[2], r.squaredd = mod$r.squared, 
      Fvald =  unname( t['value']), Fpvalued = unname( Fpvalue), 
      dfd = t['dendf'])
} # end fitdiff
```

We have been using an F-value of about 10 as the deciding factor for
diffusion. Since the diffusion is estimated via 10 points, and both an
intercept and slope are estimated, so the statistical significance of a
fit is an F distribution with 1 and 8 degrees of freedom. It may be
evaluated as `100 * pf( Fvald, 1, 8, lower.tail = FALSE)` (which
evaluates to `r100 * pf( 10, 1, 8, lower.tail = TRUE)`% significance).
1% and 5% significance levels are between F-Values of
`r c( qf( 0.05, 1, 8, lower.tail=FALSE), qf( 0.01, 1, 8, lower.tail=FALSE))`.

Finally, we want to look at the spectral width of the new sample rates
(@fig-spec).

```{r}
#| label: fig-spec
#| fig-cap: The two-sided spectral width of 99.5% of the energy of by step kinetic energy.
with( MD2DF.S[TE.mean.rs < 0.2], {
   ser=as.integer( as.factor( series))
   plot( 100*specwidth ~ TE.mean.rs, log="x", pch = ser, xlab = "Total Energy",
         ylab = "Spectral Occupancy %", col = ser)
   grid()
   lpch = 1:nlevels( as.factor( series)) # legend pch
   legend( x = "bottomleft", pch = lpch,
           legend =  levels( as.factor( series)), col = lpch)
})
```

The two-sided full spectral width $F_s$ is the sample rate (reciprocal
of the time step), and as the kinetic energy is a purely real value,
we'd be correct to say that the spectrum only goes to $F_s/2$. For
series 2 & 3, $F_s = 100/\tau$ ($\Delta t = 0.01 \tau$), and the
spectral occupancy was between 2.5 and 3%, or about $P$. For series 4
and 5, $F_s = 56.263/ \tau$ ($\Delta t = 0.0177737 \tau$). @fig-spec2
below shows this adjustment.

```{r}
#| label: fig-spec2
#| fig-cap: The two-sided spectral width of 99.5% of the energy of by step kinetic energy.

MD2DF.S[ , swoot := 100 * specwidth]
MD2DF.S[ series %in% c("S4", "S5", "S5b"), swoot := specwidth / 0.0177737]
with( MD2DF.S[TE.mean.rs < 0.2], {
   ser=as.integer( as.factor( series))
   plot( swoot ~ TE.mean.rs, log="x", pch = ser, xlab = expression( epsilon),
         ylab = expression( 1 / tau), col = ser, 
         main = "99.5% Spectral Occupancy")
   grid()
   lpch = 1:nlevels( as.factor( series)) # legend pch
   legend( x = "bottomleft", pch = lpch,
           legend =  levels( as.factor( series)), col = lpch)
})
```

It is unknown why series 2 (and 2b) had somewhat lower occupancy, but as
that code has aged out of relevancy, we will not look into it further.

# Detecting a Transition

The current literature [@Gruber2025 fig. 1; @Deutschlander2013 fig. 1]
discusses the rate of decay of the bond orientation order parameter
given by $G_6(r) = |\langle \psi^*(\vec{r}) \psi(\vec{0}) \rangle|$. Our
thought had been, without ever deriving it [@Halperin1978], that in a
small $16 \times 16$ particle system such as ours the Nelson-Halperin
order parameter $\langle \psi_6 \rangle$ would simply not decay at the
start of melting. That is, when long-range orientational order remained,
it would be measurable in $\psi_6$. As a reminder, `psiabs` is
$\langle |\psi_6| \rangle$ (the average of the magnitudes) and `psiavg`
is $|\langle \psi_6 \rangle|$ (the magnitude of the complex average).

We need to detect the first order phase change, and compare that to the
loss of long range order.

## Specific Heat via First Difference

As we move forward, we are going to ignore the series 2 data, as it had
the potential energy step at `rskn`, and the series 4 data, as it had
non-constant total energy. The specific heat at constant volume is
defined by

$$
C_v = \frac{1}{\nu}\frac{\delta E}{\delta T}
$$

where $\nu$ is the quantity of the substance (moles in real substances,
number of particles for us). Since `TE.mean.rs` and `ke.mean.rs` are
both per particle averages, we may use them directly. In computing
specific heat via the first difference, we want to combine series 3 and
3b together, and series 5 and 5b together. We need to retain the `5b`
designation though, in case we want to examine runs in detail, so we
will create a `newSeries` column that will allow the `series` column to
remain the same.

```{r}
#| label: S2
MD2DF.S2 <- MD2DF.S[ !grepl( "S2", series) & series != "S4", ] # Drop S2,S2b,S4
#MD2DF.S2[ series == "S3b", series := "S3"]

MD2DF.S2[ , rv := ke.sd.rs / ke.mean.rs] # Create relative variance column
MD2DF.S2[ is.na(hseries), `:=`(hseries = "Init", itype = "Init")] # Init S3,5,5b
MD2DF.S2[ , newSeries := fifelse( hseries == "Init", series,
                             paste( series, substr( hseries, 3, 4), sep = ""))]
MD2DF.S2[ newSeries == "S3b", newSeries := "S3"]
MD2DF.S2[ newSeries == "S5b", newSeries := "S5"]
setorder( MD2DF.S2, TE.mean.rs)
saveRDS( MD2DF.S2, file = "../MD2DF.S2.RDS") # save for future use.
```

We need to recreate and apply the $dy/dx$ function.

```{r}
#| label: dydx

dydx <- function( y, x, lag = 1) {
   # find derivative over lag + 1 points
   lx <- length( x)
   stopifnot( length( y) == lx)
   data <- data.table( x = x, y = y, keyby = x)
   xm <- (data$x[ 1:(lx - lag)] + data$x[ (lag + 1):lx]) / 2
   ym <- (data$y[ 1:(lx - lag)] + data$y[ (lag + 1):lx]) / 2
   # midpoint of eval sets
   dydxfit <- function( i) { # get dy/dx from points i:(i + lag)
      c <- coef( lm( y ~ poly( x, lag, raw = TRUE), # get poly coef
                     data = data[ i:(i + lag)]))
      dpc <- (1:lag) * tail( c, -1) # derivative of poly coeff
      polyval( rev(dpc), xm[ i]) 
      # evaluate polynomial at midpoint of data & return
   }
   dd <- vapply( 1:(lx - lag), dydxfit, 1.0)
   list( dd=dd, xm = xm, ym = ym)
}

# test
tx <- c(1, 4, 3, 3.5, 2, 5)
ty <- tx^2
(dd <- dydx(ty, tx, 2))
dd$dd - 2 * dd$xm
rm( tx, ty, dd) # remove these variables
```

Now we need to apply the function by the new series variable.
@fig-Cvbyhs below shows the result of that computation.

```{r}
#| label: fig-Cvbyhs
#| warning: false # log will produce some NaNs
#| fig-cap: First difference computation of the specific heat for each of the initialiation groups.
#| fig-height: 6.5
#| fig-width: 6.5
Cvbyhs <- by( MD2DF.S2[ , .(ke.mean.rs, TE.mean.rs, series = newSeries)], 
              MD2DF.S2[ , newSeries], 
              with, c( series = unique( substr( series, 1, 2)), 
                       dydx( TE.mean.rs, ke.mean.rs)))
# above returns a list with 11 items: one for each series
# Note that the function 'by' calls is simply 'with'.
# The `dydx()` call is passed as an extra parameter to `with`
# Each series call results in a `with( df, c( series, dd, xm))`
# The following will create a table of Log(Cv) values.
CvTable <- rbindlist( lapply( seq_along( Cvbyhs), 
                              function( i) {
   hs <- names( Cvbyhs[i]) # The series is now the name of each sublist.
   x <- Cvbyhs[[i]]
   Cvlen <- length( x$dd)
   data.table( run = rep( NA, Cvlen),
               Series = rep( hs, Cvlen),
               valid = rep( TRUE, Cvlen), # tag them all as valid
               Temp = x$xm, variable = rep( "Log(Cv)", Cvlen),
               value = log( x$dd))
   }))
xyplot( value ~ Temp | Series, data = CvTable[ Temp < 0.021],
        scales=list( y = list( relation = "free")))#, group = itype)
```

## Plot of all Data vs. Temperature

To plot all of the data, we need to make a long-form table. We need to
`melt()` the data table, but first we will create a new series variable
which will merge the `b` version of series 3, and create series from the
eight heating and cooling series. Series `5b`, on which we can do
further computations (such as $G_6(r)$), will remain distinct.

```{r}
#| label: SDFd2m


SDFd2ss <- MD2DF.S2[ , .( run, Series = newSeries, 
                       #itype, 
                       Temp = ke.mean.rs, # hseries, 
                       valid = fifelse( valid == 1, TRUE, FALSE), 
                       # Values below are those plotted, hopefully in this order
                       TE = TE.mean.rs,
                       Pressure = Pressure.mean.rs,
                       rv = ke.sd.rs / ke.mean.rs,
                       D = Estimated / 4.0, 
                       LogFpD = ifelse( Estimated < 0.0, NA, 
                                   # set lower limit, drop -D
                                   log10( pmax( 1e-15, Fpvalued))), 
                       psiavg, psiabs = psiabs.mean.rs, 
                       Cv = 1 / (1 - 256 * rv^2))]
# First select just the columns we're interested in

id.var = c( "run", "Series", "Temp", "valid") 
SDFd2m2 <- melt( SDFd2ss, id.var = id.var, #direction = 'long', 
                 variable.name = 'variable', variable.factor = TRUE,
                 value.name = 'value') 
# now each variable is its own table.

SDFd2m2 <- rbind( SDFd2m2, CvTable) # bind the Cv data table.

SDFd2m2[, `:=`(variable = factor( variable, levels = unique( variable)))]

# giving the variable factor levels will cause xyplot to NOT sort it.
setkeyv( SDFd2m2, c( "variable", "Temp"))
head( SDFd2m2)
```

The values plotted in @fig-Transition2 are as follows. `TE` is the total
energy, Pressure is calculated as

$$ 
\langle P \rangle = \rho \left( \langle T \rangle +\frac{n \langle u \rangle}{2} \right)
$$

(where $\rho, n, N, T, \text{and} u$ are the density {$1/\pi$},
potential exponent {5}, and number of particles {256}, temperature, and
average potential energy per particle, respectively), `rv` is the
relative temperature variance `rv = ke.sd.rs / ke.mean.rs`, `D` is the
measured diffusion, `LogFpD` is the common logarithm of the diffusion F
statistic probability value (the probability that the regression occurs
randomly; note that many values are smaller than $10^{-15}$), `psiabs`
is $\langle |\psi_6| \rangle$ (the average of the magnitudes) and
`psiavg` is $|\langle \psi_6 \rangle|$ (the magnitude of the complex
average), `Cv` is the specific heat computed as
$C_v = 1 / \left( 1 - \frac{N  \left< \delta T^2 \right>}{T^2} \right)$,
and `Log(Cv)` is the natural logarithm of the specific heat computed as
the first difference by series )note this is not the logarithm of the
data in the `Cv` panel).

```{r}
#| label: fig-Transition2
#| fig-cap: Statistics around transition plotted against temperature. See text for description of statistics.
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-width: 6.5

xlim <- c(0.0069, 0.016)
pltdata <- copy( SDFd2m2[ Temp %within% xlim,])
gps <- length( unique( pltdata$Series))
pchs <- rep_len( 0:6, length.out = gps)
cols <- rep(  c("darkred", "darkgreen", "darkblue"), each = 7, 
                  length.out = gps)
xyplot(
  value ~ Temp | variable, 
  data = pltdata,
  groups = Series,      # <-- tell lattice to use Series as groups
  subscripts = TRUE,
  as.table = TRUE,
  scales = list( y = list( relation = "free")),
  xlab = "Temperature",
  main = "Key Statistics Around Transition vs. T",
  par.settings = list( superpose.symbol = list( pch = pchs, col = cols)),
  auto.key = list( columns = 3),   # <-- legend appears
 
  panel = function(x, y, subscripts, groups, ...) 
     {
    panel.grid(h = -1, v = -1)
    panel.superpose( x, y, subscripts = subscripts, groups = groups,
                     panel.groups = function(x, y, ...) {
                        panel.xyplot(x, y, ...)}, ...)
      } # end panel = function...
)
```

## Plot of all Data vs. Total Energy

We must redo the melt to get the table based on `TE`. This includes
recomputing `CvTable` and `SDFd2m2`.

```{r}
#| label: SDFd2m3
CvTable2 <- rbindlist( lapply( seq_along( Cvbyhs), 
                              function( i) {
   hs <- names( Cvbyhs[i]) # The series is now in the name of this sublist.
   x <- Cvbyhs[[i]]
   Cvlen <- length( x$dd)
   data.table( run = rep( NA, Cvlen), #itype = rep( x$itype, Cvlen),
               Series = rep( hs, Cvlen),
               valid = rep( TRUE, Cvlen), # we'll declare all valid
               TE = x$ym, variable = rep( "Log(Cv)", Cvlen),
               value = log( x$dd))
   }))

# First select just the columns we're interested in

id.var = c( "run", "Series", "TE", "valid")
SDFd2m3 <- melt( SDFd2ss, id.var = id.var, direction = 'long', 
                 variable.name = 'variable', variable.factor = TRUE,
                 value.name = 'value') 
# now each variable is its own table.

SDFd2m3 <- rbind( SDFd2m3, CvTable2) # bind the Cv data table.

SDFd2m3[, `:=`(variable = factor( variable, levels = unique( variable)))]#,
# giving the variable factor levels will cause xyplot to NOT sort it.
setkeyv( SDFd2m3, c( "variable", "TE"))
head( SDFd2m3)
```

Note that there are a few points which have `LogFpD` value below -1,

higher temperatures might find themselves moving away from their lattice
positions and then returning. `D = .001` is about as small as real
diffusion gets (although, `S3.0044h06`, at $D =  0.00051$, is certainly

## Defining Transitions

Back in [FinalDiffusion.pdf](FinalDiffusion.pdf) we defined a series of
functions to detect phase transitions. These are now in the file
`detect.r` and are simply document, but the definitions are not echoed
due to their length. The main function is
`detect( data, nsig = 3, nstart = 10, level = 0.99)`, where data is an
MD2DF `data.table` melted into a form here exemplified by `SDFd2m2`
(that is, with `Temp` as the independent variable), `nsig` is the number
of standard deviations for the `stepdet()` function to detect start of
diffusion, `nstart` is the number of points to include in the start of
running means or regression lines, `level` is the significance threshold
to exceed to call a line departure a detection. `detect()` returns a
vector of temperatures at which detections occurred, and a string vector
describing each detection.

```{r}
#| label: detectR
#| 
source("./detect.r")
```

This function performs eight detections.

-   `diff`: Finds the coldest item which deviates three standard
    deviations starting with the first `nstart` items.
-   `maxCv`: Item with the maximum Cv as computed by relative variance.
-   `maxLCv`: Item with the maximum Cv as computed by the base-ten
    logarithm of first difference of total energy vs. temperature.
-   `Maxrv`: Item with the maximum relative variance.
-   `LogFpD`: Coldest item whose diffusion regression F statistic
    p-value is below 1% (i.e., all calculated in logarithms).
-   `Icld1`: These three use `linedet()` to find a deviation above 1%
    confidence of a line fit to pressures vs. temperature. The first
    looks for the Solid 1 to Solid 2 transition.
-   `Icld2`: Looks starting from `Icld1` for a 0.001% deviation.
-   `Icld3`: Looks in reverse for the hottest 1% deviation (find
    transition in reverse.)

@tbl-onedet shows the result of one detection.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-onedet
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: Series 3 transition temperature detections.
knitr::kable( detect( SDFd2m2[ Series == "S3"], luc = "Temp", nstart = 5))
```

This is almost identical to the prior results:

```         
diff     maxCv    maxLCv   Maxrv    LogFp    Icld1   Icld2     Icld3
0.012832 0.013006 0.013000 0.013006 0.012832 0.007971 0.012832 0.013104
```

As can be seen, `MaxLCv` is now detected slightly lower. Unsure why this
is different. This detection is simply the maximum of the `Log(Cv)`
variable, calculated as the first difference in `Cvbyhs` above. It is
possible that the prior results did not include the `S3b` results,
although I thought they did. It is difficult to go back and verify this,
although not impossible. The function computing `maxLCv` is simply the R
function `which.max()`, applied to the the data in @fig-Cvbyhs above, so
there is little risk.

Using the `detect()` function on each series and stuffing the results in
a long-form `data.table` is accomplished by the following:

```{r}
#| label: detecths
dhs <- rbindlist( 
          lapply( levels( factor( SDFd2m2$Series)), 
                  function( x) { 
                     dt <- detect( SDFd2m2[ Series == x,], nstart = 5, 
                               luc = "Temp")
                     dt[, Series := x]}))
dhs[, Series := as.factor( Series)]
dhs[, variable := as.factor( variable)]
setkey( dhs, Series)
#knitr::kable( dhs)
```

We can see these results in @tbl-dhs.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dhs
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: Detected transitions in series 3 and 5. All values are temperature in scaled units.  The cooling series (`S343` through `S346`) did not have enough energy steps above the transition to be detected from above, so the `Icld3` items are `NA`.
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')
knitr::kable( dcast( dhs, Series ~ variable, value.var = "value"))
```

That is an unsatisfying result. First, `Icld1` which was supposed to
detect the first solid-to-solid transition, is at different
temperatures. We knew that this might be the case for the
heating/cooling series, as the steps there were large, but series 3 and
5 should agree, and it is not clear that they do. Second, the series 5
data detects `Icld2` a transition at $T=0.011$ (both detections look for
statistically significant deviations from a regression line; 1%
significance for `Icld1`, and 0.001% for `Icld2`, the second search
started after the first).

@tbl-dhse shows the percent error of each value. The heating and cooling
series did not have terribly many runs, and so the temperature
uncertainties were typically larger.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-dhse
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: Error in detected transitions as a percentage of their value in series 3 and 5. The error is simply the temperature distance between adjacent runs sorted by temperature, so the `S3` and `S5` series, which have very many runs, generally have lower uncertainties.
options(knitr.kable.NA = '')
knitr::kable( dcast( dhs[, "%err" := 100*delx/value], 
                     Series ~ variable, value.var = "%err"))
```

We can see the detected transitions for each series plotted in @fig-dets
below.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dets
#| fig-cap: Detection plotted for each series, values are temperatures.  The series are numbered 1 - 10 in the order of the legend (`S3` - `S5`).

# Code from Chat GPT
## example: dhs already exists with Series as factor
## dhs = data.table(Series = factor(...), variable=..., value=..., delx=...)

pfun <- function(x, y, subscripts, groups, ...) {
  ## d is the half-height of the error bar for each row in this panel
  d_full <- dhs$delx[subscripts] / 2

  panel.superpose( x, y, subscripts = subscripts, groups = groups, 
                   panel.groups = 
      function(x, y, subscripts, col, pch, ...) {
      ## convert factor positions -> numeric plotting positions
      x_num <- as.numeric(x)   # e.g. factor levels -> 1,2,3,...

      ## Use dhs values for delx (indexed by the subscripts from outer panel)
      d <- d_full  # already aligned to subscripts
      panel.points(x_num, y, col = col, pch = pch, ...)
    }, # end panel.groups()
    ... # any other arguments to panel.groups()
  ) # close paren on panel.superpose()
} # pfun()

## Create the plot: value on y, Series (factor) on x, panel per variable
xyplot( value ~ Series | variable, data = dhs, groups = Series,
        panel = pfun,
        auto.key = TRUE,
        xlab = "Series", ylab = "Temperature",
        scales = list( x = list( at = seq_along( levels( dhs$Series)), 
                              labels = seq_along( levels( dhs$Series)))))
```

There is some consistency there, although Series `S5` stands out in the
`LogFpD` and `Icld3` detections, and perhaps in `maxCv`. This may be
because there were two full runs in series 5, resulting in 210 total
runs. Thus, `LogFpD`, with a 1% threshold, could just be bad luck (i.e.,
a detection due to noise). It might be interesting to combine all of the
series 3 data too (ignoring the heating/cooling).

# Changing MD2RP to Return 2/3 Tail

The non-valid data with long runs have relatively small slopes.
@fig-S2TRvFval shows the not-valid runs total ranges as a

```{r}
#| label: fig-S2TRvFval
#| fig-cap: The total temperature range predicted by the temperature linear regression (`100 * Estimate * nr / ke.mean.rs`) plotted against the F statistic value (values greater than one are considerd not-valid; greater than 10 are increasingly unlikely to be a linear correlation by random chance). 
with( MD2DF.S2[ valid != 1], {
   ser=as.integer( as.factor( series))
   plot( 100 * Estimate * nr / ke.mean.rs ~ Fval, log="x", pch = ser, ylab = "T Total Range")
   grid()
   legend( x = "bottomleft", pch = 1:nlevels( as.factor( series)), 
           legend =  levels( as.factor( series)))
})
```

Having modified `findlmlen()` to skip a fraction `skpfrac = 1/3` of the
record after `skplen` if the run is not declared valid (vs. returning
the whole record after `skplen`), we need to re-run `MD2DFfile()` on
series 5b. We will simplify the database name in memory too, dropping
the "DF", and changing the name on disk to have the `MD2DT` prefix (as
it is a `data.table` not a `dtd.frame`), and we will restart the
numbering with `A`. Out of view of this document, the `MD2RP` package
was checked and built, and installed with
`devtools::install("/home/phil/MD/MD2RP")`, and the whole document was
restarted.

```{r}
#| label: MD2A
system.time( MD2.A <- MD2DFfile( "../MD2DT.A.RDS", td, "S5b.*.scalars.csv",
                                 skpfrac = 1/3))
```

Original run time (pretty fast, as `*.rfdt.RDS` files already exist).

```         
4179  files found.
   user  system elapsed 
  0.263   0.074  41.645 
```

We can compare the new result with the prior (@fig-S2aA).

```{r}
#| label: fig-S2aA
#| fig-cap: Plot old and new relative temperature drift in percent for non-valid runs.  Note that the order of the points themselves are quite different, as the new regressions have about 1/3 less points.
with( MD2DF.S2[ series == "S5b" & valid != 1], {
   ser=as.integer( as.factor( series))
   plot( 100 * Estimate * nr / ke.mean.rs ~ Fval, log="x", pch = 4,
         main = "Temperature Drift", ylab = "% Relative Drift in T")
   grid()
   legend( x = "bottomleft", pch = 4, legend =  c( "Original", "New"), 
           col = c("black", "red"))
})
with( MD2.A[ valid != 1], {
   ser=as.integer( as.factor( series))
   points( 100 * Estimate * nr / ke.mean.rs ~ Fval, pch = 4, 
           col = "red")
})
```

A direct comparison can be made by joining the two tables. @fig-re shows
the relative slope change as a percentage of the original slope.

```{r}
#| label: fig-re
#| fig-cap: Relative percentage change in temperature slope estimate of not-valid runs in series S5b when shortening the runs to trailing 2/3 steps. Plotted against original temperature.
dt3 <- merge( MD2DF.S2, MD2.A, by = "run", all.x = FALSE)
plot( re ~ Temp, ylab = "Percentage slope change",
      data = dt3[valid.x != 1 & ke.mean.rs.x < 0.02, 
                 .(re = 100 * (Estimate.x - Estimate.y) / Estimate.x,
                   Temp = ke.mean.rs.x, Estimate.x)])
grid()
```

The average temperature will also have changed, but not by much.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dT
#| fig-cap: Percentage average temperature change resulting from different averaging lengths for not-valid runs in series S5b, on logarithmic scale. The maximum value is about 0.6%.
plot( abs(100*(ke - Temp)/Temp) ~ Temp, ylab = "% Change", log="y",
      main = "% Avereage Temp. Change",
      data = dt3[valid.x != 1 & ke.mean.rs.x < 0.02, 
                 .(Temp = ke.mean.rs.x, ke = ke.mean.rs.y)], ylim=c(1e-5,1))
grid()
```

To complete this process, we need to merge the two tables, this time
keeping the older series too. The code below will accomplish this, and
it will only be run by hand.

```{r}
#| label: MD2DT.B
#| eval: false

# we won't eval this at each document process pass.
MD2.B <- copy( MD2DF.S2)
setkey( MD2.B, run)
setkey( MD2.A, run)
MD2.B[ MD2.A, (names( MD2.A)) := mget( paste0( "i.", names( MD2.A)))]
saveRDS( MD2.B, "../MD2DT.B.RDS")
```

As a reminder, the series 2 and 4 data have been removed from this data
table, as neither is considered reliable (series two had the potential
energy step, and series 4 total energy was not constant).

# Series Database

Until now, we have focused on runs, with data collected for each run.
The detected transitions though are a temperature which applies to whole
series. The `detect()` function should not be run over the whole data
frame, but only series by series. The `hdf5r` package on
(CRAN)\[https://cran.r-project.org/\]

```{r}
require( hdf5r)
f <- list.files( td, "S5b.00126.0003.jld2", full.names = TRUE)
f1 <- H5File$new( f, mode = "r") # open read-only
names( f1)
f1sr <- f1[["SystemRecord"]]
f1srd <- f1sr[] # why this works is a mystery
f1srd
f1[["MD2version"]][] # Version info
f1$close_all()
```

The data is brought in as a data frame, so it should be easy to import
all files in a series. Note that nothing in the `SystemRecord` data
indicates anything about initialization or heating and cooling. The file
records the state of the system, which is inherent in the positions and
velocities of the particles.

-   `N`: the number of particles. You need this to read in the particle
    positions and velocities.
-   `n`: the potential energy exponent. The potential field is
    $E = 1/r^n - 1/r_s^n$, where $r$ is the distance between two
    particles and $r_s$ is the "skin" distance (see `rskn` below).
-   `totalsteps`: the total number of time steps the system had been
    propagated since initialization or the last heating/cooling cycle.
-   `tau`: the time step. This is the primary difference between the
    previous series and series 5.
-   `shell`: the range in which particles are tracked for possible
    interaction.
-   `ishell`: this is used in the calculation `ishell` =
    `shell`$/\sqrt{2}$.
-   `rskn`: the potential energy range $r_s$.
-   `iskn`: used in calculation like `ishell`; `iskn` = $r_s/\sqrt{2}$
-   `skip`: number of time steps between re-correlating the interacting
    particles.
-   `bx` & `by`: The box size. `bx` $\ge$ `by`

The objects `p` & `v` are the positions and velocities of the particles,
but wee won't try to unpack these here. What is missing is the
precision, which will be either `Float64` or `Float32` (even `Float16`
is available in *Julia*). I used `h5dump`, but I cannot find where this
is encoded in the file, other than in all of the real types. `JLD2`
encodes these as `H5T_IEEE_F64LE` or `H5T_IEEE_F32LE`, but R's `hdf5R`
package simply brings them in as doubles. I think this will have to be
recorded by hand, as will the propagation scheme used (Verlet, or
Velocity Verlet).

We can determine these things by simply reading in a record in *julia*:

```{julia}
#| label: readMD
#| eval: false
julia> MD2.readMDRecord(joinpath( datadir, "S5b.00126.0003.jld2"))
-----ReadMDRecord(), Current MD2 Version 1.6.11
Restoring system on 2026-01-14T08:02:05.150
System State restored from /media/phil/Original/Users/phils/Documents/DSP/MD/Data/1980/S5b.00126.0003.jld2, timestamp: 2025-11-11T15:00:40.979, Restored from MD2 Version: 1.6.3
Current total steps: 11000
Total Kinetic Energy: 4.0058613, T = 0.015647896
Type of MDRecord: Main.MD2.MDRecordVV{Float32}
Linear Momentum: Float32[-1.915876f-6, 7.981202f-6]
Angular Momentum: -51.23612
Main.MD2.MDRecordVV{Float32} with parameters:
 N: 256
 n: 5
 total steps: 11000
 tau: 0.0177737
 shell: 5.0
 rskn: 3.5
 skip: 50
 bx: 15.237005
 by: 13.195634
 Calculated Density: 0.31830987
 Hexagonal grid spacing: 1.9046257
 NHOPr: 2.601767
```

A few other calculated parameters are also given. The record type is
`Main.MD2.MDRecordVV{Float32}`, so it was run with Velocity Verlet
propagation and is a `Float32` implementation. Unfortunately, this only
works for fairly recent versions, as the `S1` and `S2` series `.jld2`
files will not open with the new version. `h5dump` can still be used
though to see the parameters. Older version all used the Verlet
propagation. Note that we lost the series 3 and 4 files, so these will
have to be reconstructed from the notes. Series 1 data is not stored as
a single data table, but as a data table in an environment, so rather
than pollute the notebook's environment, the total steps where
calculated outside the notebook and and simply inserted below.

```{r}
#| label: SeriesDF
SeriesDF1 <- data.frame( c(series = "S5", prop = "VV", prec = "Float32", 
                      f1srd[c("N", "n","totalsteps", "tau", "shell", "rskn", 
                              "skip", "bx", "by")]))
SeriesDF1[ 1, "totalsteps"] <- MD2DF.S2[grepl( "S5", series), sum(total.steps)]
s1 <- SeriesDF1[ 1,]
s1$series <- "S1"
s1$prop <- "V"
s1$prec <- "Float64"
s1$tau = 0.01
s1$totalsteps <- 3300000 # load( "~/MD/MD2/MD2DF.S1.Rdata") then
                         # sum( MD2DF$total.steps)
SeriesDF1 <- rbind( SeriesDF1, s1)
s2 <- SeriesDF1[ 2, ] # copy second row as it's closer.
s2$series <- "S2"
s2$totalsteps <- MD2DF.Q6[grepl( "S2", series), sum(total.steps)]
s3 <- s2
s3$series <- "S3"
s3$totalsteps <- MD2DF.S2[grepl( "S3", series), sum(total.steps)]
s4 <- SeriesDF1[ 1,] # S4 is closer to S5
s4$series <- "S4"
s4$prop <- "V"
s4$totalsteps <- MD2DF.S[grepl( "S4", series), sum(total.steps)]
SeriesDF1 <- rbind( SeriesDF1, s2, s3, s4)
```

The result is below in @tbl-SDF1.

```{r}
#| tbl-cap: Series data frame.
#| echo: false
knitr::kable( SeriesDF1, format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```
